stages.name: Poverty and inequality
stages.title: Poverty and inequality
stages.sub: How we measure poverty, and how growth and inequality together decide whether it falls.

steps.q: A country has 1,000 people and 200 of them live below the $2.15-a-day line. What single figure tells you how widespread poverty is here?
steps.right: The percentage of people below the line
steps.wrong: The average income of everyone in the country
steps.hint: You want a share of the population, not an average.

steps.q: Two countries both have 20% of people below the poverty line. In Country A those people earn just under the line, in Country B they earn half the line. Does the headcount ratio tell you which country's poor are worse off?
steps.right: No, it looks the same in both
steps.hint: The headcount ratio only counts how many people are below the line, not how far below.

steps.q: The absolute poverty line stays fixed at $2.15 a day. If real GDP rises and wages across the country rise with it, what happens to the number of people earning under $2.15?
steps.right: It falls, as incomes rise above the fixed line
steps.wrong: It stays the same, since the line has not moved
steps.hint: The line does not move, but incomes do. Who crosses it?

steps.q: The relative poverty line is 60% of median income. If the richest households' incomes rise sharply while the median barely moves, does the relative poverty line change even though nobody's actual income has fallen?
steps.right: Yes, the line rises because the median can shift with it
steps.wrong: No, the line only depends on the poorest households
steps.hint: The relative line is tied to the middle of the income scale, not to any single group's income.

steps.q: Real GDP grows by 5%, but almost all of the extra income goes to the richest 10% while the median household's income barely rises. Does relative poverty (below 60% of median) fall just because the economy grew?
steps.right: Not necessarily, it depends on who gains from the growth
steps.wrong: Yes, any growth automatically lowers it
steps.hint: Growth raises absolute incomes, but relative poverty depends on the median and how gains are shared.
